passage: During the Diwali puja the lights went out just as the aarti began. Madhav, five, stood beside his grandfather Shankar in the dark. Shankar lit the lamp and moved it in slow circles while the family sang. Madhav copied by waving his hands in circles. "Why do we do circles?" "To show respect and say thank you, and to welcome the light." "So the lamp is like a hello." "You could say so."

qa.q: What happened just as the aarti began?
qa.a: The lights went out.

qa.q: What might Madhav be feeling when he says the lamp is like a hello?
qa.a: Curious, and pleased to make sense of it in his own way. He may still be unsure what it all means.

qa.q: How did Shankar help the meaning grow beyond copying?
qa.a: He explained in a few simple words why they do it and welcomed Madhav's own way of putting it.

qa.q: How might Shankar feel watching Madhav copy him in the dark?
qa.a: Calm and touched, since he kept the lamp moving and answered gently.

grounding: Shows a young child copying an aarti and asking why, with an adult explaining what the ritual marks.

passage: The cake had five candles. Leela, five, stared as the family sang and her mother Seema dimmed the lights. "Make a wish, but don't tell." Leela shut her eyes tight, then blew, and the smoke curled up. "Why do we blow?" "It's our way of marking a new year and wishing you well." Leela watched the smoke. "Did my wish go up?" Seema smiled. "Maybe. Let's cut the cake."

qa.q: How many candles were on the cake?
qa.a: Five.

qa.q: What might Leela be thinking as she watches the smoke?
qa.a: Wondering whether her wish travelled up, with curiosity and perhaps hope.

qa.q: How could Seema help the meaning of the ritual grow?
qa.a: Give short simple reasons for it and welcome Leela's own ideas about the wish.

qa.q: How might Seema feel at this moment?
qa.a: Happy and tender, since she smiled at the question.

grounding: Shows a young child watching a birthday song and candles and asking what the ritual means.

passage:
“Sangeeta Aunty, why are you going round and round with the lamp?”
Asif stood at the neighbours' door during Diwali, watching the aarti.
Sangeeta smiled. “In our family, we move the lamp in circles to say thank you and show love to God. The light means goodness.”
“Can I watch?”
“Of course.”
The bell rang, and everyone sang. Asif stood very still.
Afterwards he said, “At Eid we light lamps too, on the balcony.”
“Light is special for lots of families,” said Sangeeta, and gave him a laddoo.

qa.q: Why does Sangeeta's family move the lamp in circles?
qa.a: To say thank you and show love to God.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling as he watched the aarti?
qa.a: He was curious and respectful, standing very still, and then felt connected when he remembered his own family's lamps.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta help the ritual mean more to Asif?
qa.a: She explained simply why her family does it, so he understood more than just the actions.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta feel when Asif mentions Eid lamps?
qa.a: She likely feels warm and pleased that he saw something shared between their families.

grounding: A child watches a neighbour's aarti and learns why the ritual matters, connecting it to his own family's festival.

passage:
Note by Saurabh, KG teacher.
Today was Siddharth's birthday. When we sang and he blew out the candles, he asked, “Why do we blow them?” I said, “In many families, it's a way to mark that you're one year older and to make a wish.” He thought, then asked if he could blow them again for his friend's birthday next week. I told him the candles belong to the birthday child, but he could sing loudest. He practised singing all afternoon.

qa.q: What did Siddharth ask if he could do next week?
qa.a: Blow the candles again for his friend's birthday.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling when he asked why they blow the candles?
qa.a: He was curious about the ritual, wanting to understand it, not just copy it.

qa.q: How did Saurabh help the ritual's meaning grow?
qa.a: Saurabh explained simply that it marks being a year older and making a wish, and that the candles belong to the birthday child.

qa.q: How might Siddharth's friend feel next week?
qa.a: The friend would likely feel special, blowing the candles while Siddharth sings loudest.

grounding: The teacher's note shows a preschooler asking why birthday candles are blown and learning the meaning behind the ritual.

passage: At the first harvest, Omkar Dada carried the first bundle of wheat to the edge of the field and placed it under the neem tree with a lamp. Ira watched, holding her mother's hand. “Why are you giving wheat to the tree, Dada?” He knelt. “It's our way of saying thank you, to the earth and the rain, before we eat.” Ira thought. “Like saying thank you for food?” “Exactly.” Ira picked up a single grain and put it next to the bundle. “My thank you.”

qa.q: Where did Dada place the first bundle of wheat?
qa.a: Under the neem tree, with a lamp.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling when she added her own grain?
qa.a: She felt proud and included, wanting to give her own thank you after understanding the ritual.

qa.q: What did Dada do that helped the ritual mean more than imitation?
qa.a: He explained simply that it was a way of saying thank you to the earth and rain, linking it to something Ira knew.

qa.q: How might Dada feel when Ira adds her grain?
qa.a: He likely feels moved and happy that she understood and joined in.

grounding: A child watches a harvest ritual and learns from her grandfather why it matters, adding her own thank you.

passage: In Seville, the whole family squeezed round Bisabuela's table. Someone switched off the lights, and a cake crowded with candles glowed. Everyone sang, and Bisabuela blew. Tomas watched the smoke curl up and frowned. "Why did we put fire on the cake and then blow it away?" His mother, Fatima, pulled him onto her lap. "Each candle is a year Bisabuela has lived. We sing because we're glad she's here, and blowing them out means a new year starts." Tomas thought about it. Later he stuck a crayon into his toast, sang to his toy rabbit and whispered, "Happy new year of being here."

qa.q: What did Tomas stick into his toast?
qa.a: He stuck a crayon into his toast.

qa.q: What does Tomas's frown as the smoke curled up suggest?
qa.a: He was most likely puzzled about why fire goes on a cake only to be blown away. He might also have felt a little uneasy about the flames.

qa.q: Which choice helped Tomas understand the ritual, and why?
qa.a: Fatima explained in a few simple words what the candles and the song mean, so Tomas could repeat the ritual with its meaning, as he did with his rabbit.

qa.q: How might Bisabuela feel when the whole family sings round her?
qa.a: She would likely feel loved and glad to be celebrated by everyone squeezed round her table.

grounding: It illustrates a young child watching a birthday candle ritual and an adult's explanation helping its meaning grow beyond copying.
